text: We have eaten at many a fancy restaurant and this had to be one of our top 20 dining experiences. Not just because the food was delicious--and it was, dear reader, oh how delicious it was--but because of the pleasure of the entire experience. We were there for our 15th wedding anniversary, and we felt supremely well taken care of by the staff--from the friendly call a few hours beforehand confirming our reservation, to the greeting at the door when we arrived, to the way several of the staff introduced themselves to us, to our extremely knowledgeable and enthusiastic waiter Hunter (hi Hunter!), to the perfectly timed visits from the busboys, to the way they let us linger as long as we wanted after our meal was over, the staff made our experience a pleasure. The rose petals on our table was a nice anniversary touch too. The decor was pretty without being stuffy or pompous and our table was in a nice quiet corner, not too close to others but close enough that we could occasionally chat across the aisle to comment on each others' desserts. :) My only tiny complaint was that the music occasionally felt a bit too raucous and intrusive (James Brown in a fine dining experience felt a little off--much as I love James Brown). Ok now on to the food! We wanted to taste as many things as possible so we shared all our dishes and Hunter suggested half glasses of different wines to go with each course. His wine pairings were PERFECT and this was one of the best parts of the meal for us, especially since we really didn't know anything about Santa Barbara wines. We started with Savory Foie Gras and Milles-Feuilles mushroom puff pastry as appetizers, along with a Melville Pinot Noir that complemented them nicely. The Foie Gras was melty smooth but firm and so tasty with its sauce and the multi-layered mushroom pastry was also quite good (though difficult to cut up and share). After that we had the Mixed Greens organic salad with cheese, marcona almonds, apricots, and pumpkin vinaigrette, along with a lovely white wine whose name is currently escaping me. Then we shared the tangerine-seared scallops with shrimp risotto, prosciutto and pea coulis, along with a delicious fruity Melville white (viogner?) whose name is also escaping me. The scallops were perfectly cooked and the risotto nice and creamy--I "yum!"ed through every bite. After that was their signature bourbon-and-maple-glazed duck breast + confit over a succotash of corn, fava beans, bacon and butternut squash, and my "yum" noises went up a notch. Both the duck breast and the confit were done perfectly and the glaze was just the right consistency and combination of flavors. With the duck we had another pinot noir from Santa Maria whose name is sadly also escaping me. After the main courses settled we split two desserts: the molten lava chocolate cake with Brazilian coffee ice cream and their signature blueberry upside down cake with lemon zest ice cream. Both were terrific but the blueberry cake was an especially nice combo of flavors. We had a dessert wine with this which was also perfectly paired but of course....its name is now escaping me (dang). They also had an impressive cheese course menu (I love a restaurant that has a cheese course for dessert) with a lot of Northern California cheeses, but since we're from there and the Cowgirl Creamery is immediately accessible to us, we declined that course (I recommend it for others though, their selections were great--Mt. Tam, Red Hawk, Humboldt Fog, etc are all delicious). We really really enjoyed this meal and I would heartily recommend it to any foodie looking for a fabulous fine dining experience without the formal stuffy feeling. Thank you Bouchon for making our anniversary a special one!

text: Holy crap, this place is spectacular. I have been here for the omakase many times over the years and am always blown away. I have been to comparable (and sometimes more expensive) restaurants in other cities and with the exception of Nobu in NYC, which is pretty similar in its awesomeness, there is just nothing that competes both in terms of food quality and quality of service. If you are ordering a la carte, I highly recommend the ishi yaki bop with kobe beef (or, if you are feeling really really decadent, upgrade to wagyu). It is a singular dish - extremely yummy, and something you can't get anywhere else. I have also heard good things about the Sea Bass. They have a great selection of sakes, some of which are Morimoto house sakes, and they are great at matching you with a sake based on your preferences. Morimoto is not really known for its dessert, so I wouldn't recommend coming just for dessert, though. That said, let's get on to the important part: the omakase. First of all, paying more really does make a difference. The most expensive omakase grade is completely worth it - I find the $80 to be a bit lackluster by comparison. The same goes for the beverage omakase. I have tried both the general beverage omakase and the sake omakase and in both cases, they have been superbly matched with the courses (this is particularly true for the more expensive courses paired with the more expensive beverage omakases - at lower levels, it's more like some tasty drinks and some tasty food but they aren't perfectly matched up). Even better than there just being fantastic food, I have almost always had superb waiters who are familiar with the food I am eating, as well as the drink pairings (they either selected the pairings themselves or have tried them) and can talk with us at length about what we are eating. It is worth noting, for the lady who gave the place 3 stars because she didn't love one of the dishes, if you are honest with the waiter when he asks you how you like each course, HE WILL BRING YOU ANOTHER COURSE. They don't mind. They know you are paying a lot and want you to be happy with your experience. I have found Morimoto to be nothing but pure class. One time, a bug got in my glass of sake 2/3 of the way into my carafe and in apology, they brought me an entirely new, full carafe of sake. If you are really into food, you will have a great time doing the omakase. I have had a particularly good experience with a server whose name is, I believe, Dan? text: I'm not much of a Malaysian food expert, but, hot damn I loved this place. I don't know whether Penang qualifies as "authentic" or not, but all I know is that Penang served up some of the most delicious food I've ever tasted. Hyperbole much? I don't think so. My dinner companion and I stepped in here on a frigid Tuesday evening. Although the streets were empty outside, Penang was buzzing with both conventioneers and locals. The space was quite large with a quick turnover of tables, we were able to get a choice spot overlooking the open kitchen. It was a great atmosphere to browse the sprawling menu while sipping the complementary hot tea. Although the staff seemed a little frenzied, they were always prompt and polite. Our server was quick to take our appetizer order, so we started dinner with the following-- * Roti canai. These crispy Malaysian-style "pancakes" were delicious. They came with a curry sauce for dipping, which made for a decadent (albeit messy) start to dinner. * Tofu satay. Massive tofu pieces crisped to perfection, served with a generous pile peanut sauce with cucumbers mixed in. This was probably my favorite item of the night. Next up, the entrees. We both settled for noodle dishes and ate family style, to maximize the opportunities for sharing-- * Chow kueh teow. Basically, these are rice noodles stir-fried in chili and soy and tossed with squid and shrimp. Although I'm not a seafood fan, I was completely surprised by how delicious this one was. The noodles were crispy and flavorful, and the dish didn't taste "fishy" at all. * Beef chow fun. A classic -- beef with flat noodles and sprouts. This was outstanding too. The beef was crispy and spicy, and nothing like the greasy-spoon beef chow fun that I'm used to. Four dishes -- and four home runs. Sounds like a five-star dinner to me. A five-star dinner that was also dirt-cheap (dinner for two amounted to a mere $20 + tip). Nice. No doubt I'll be back here the next time I'm in town.

I think the most disappointing thing about this place was the fact that the breakfast menu was really limited at lunch time. The decor needs some big-time upgrading, but that's honestly not unique to this diner in particular (it seems to be a common problem among them). text: My first impression was of trying to reach this compound on foot from McGavock Pike. A sidewalk was provided; "That's thoughtful," I said to myself, since getting run over seemed a likely alternative. The more the sidewalk meandered about the grounds, however, the more doubts I began to have. When the sidewalk led me to a closed, locked gate, "thoughtful" was no longer the word I associated with it. Fortunately, an entrance (excuse me, "portico") was visible only a quarter-mile away, and at that point I disregarded the "Please follow sidewalk" signs and went for the shortest distance between two points. My second impression was of a cozy, high-class hotel lobby -- I'd entered through the Magnolia Portico. My third, as I traveled toward my meeting room, was of the enormous Delta Atrium, full of plants, brick buildings, wrought iron railings, flowing water and winding paths and overlooked by walls of balconied hotel rooms. It had a quirky, organic charm. My fourth impression was of trying to find a decent place to eat dinner. I was in a gregarious mood and happened to strike up a conversation with two other convention-goers, which is the only reason I got into Volare, which had one unreserved table left and a 90-minute (!) anticipated wait after that. (The next night I tried, and failed, to get into Wasabi, a seafood restaurant, and I balked at the outrageously expensive Old Hickory Steakhouse.) Some of Volare's entrees were appealing-looking but, at $20 to $30, out of my range. I settled for a Caesar salad and a personal brick-oven pizza, which I ate half of. When I asked to have the other half wrapped up, the waiter brought me a Pizza Hut box. He said it had come from room service, but I still had to go, "Hmmm." My fifth impression was that, once inside the compound, it was difficult to get out. I was staying in a motel just across McGavock Pike, less than a mile away, but a taxi ride from one side to the other (no way was I going to attempt to walk the distance anymore) cost $7; a ride to anywhere else in town had to be at least $15. (I discovered later that it cost twice that to get to the Vanderbilt-Belmont area.) Also -- sixth impression -- the artificiality of the place was starting to get to me. It had been cute at first, but the tourist-trap ambience of Delta Island in particular and the extremely expensive array of available shops and restaurants in general, not to mention the tacky Christmas decorations (in mid-November -- pretty soon, the World Series and the start of the winter holiday season are going to cross over each other), had eclipsed it. In two days, I'd learned my way around the labyrinth pretty well, and since my mind was no longer occupied by figuring out how to get from Point A to Point B, it now had time to notice -- and dwell on -- what a colossal pain in the ass it invariably was. It began to feel like one of those Star Trek bubble universes, where the laws of physics are different and people disappear and undulating girls in tight, skimpy black dresses sing "We Got the Beat" and "Wrap It Up" in a faux Bourbon Street bar. I was sorely tempted, more than once, to toss a wrapper on the path, just to test the level of surveillance. My seventh and final impression was that Findley's Allegedly Irish Pub was the only decent meal deal in the entire joint -- a tasty crab cake with remoulade and pub chips cost around $10. Also, if you came at night, a couple of guys (one from Tennessee, one from Leicestershire) would play Irish songs and crack jokes about how ridiculous the "Bayou-dome" was. (Not that Findley's itself escaped this ridiculousness -- among the menu items was, I kid you not, the Pail o' Sausage.) In five days, I managed to escape from the bubble into the real world only once. I can state authoritatively that the real world is better.

text: I have to say that I cannot look at this place's lamely punned name without feeling a twinge of embarrassment on its behalf. Does the term "douchechills" apply here? I'm not sure. Although the place was almost empty, we were seated cheek to jowl with another group, resulting in two parties with two servers having to yell over one another. The menu has a small list of drinks and a long list of dishes, and my friends and I had to ask some questions to make heads or tails of it - thankfully, our server was nice and super helpful. The water filling people and table bussing people were omnipresent and maybe too attentive, grabbing at plates that were still half full. If you ate at Du Jour, you know what the space looks like - just imagine everything painted purple and orange, plus a big, cool-looking, lit up communal table in the middle. I would like to offer a fist bump to whoever's in charge of the soundtrack. Lots of Cure, and was that Love & Rockets I heard above the din? Ah, my day just got a little better. Have you ever seen a potato leek spring roll before? I hadn't either, and I'll avoid them if I do again, because they tasted mostly like straight grease. The gingery Vietnamese roll was on the opposite end of the deliciousness spectrum, with lots of flavor and a kick-ass sauce that managed to be salty, sweet and spicy all at once. The main dishes were also really up and down in terms of quality - my friend's yellow curry was good. My fried rice (wait, "wok-fried tofu and vegetables") came out of the kitchen underseasoned, but that was quickly remedied with the tasty homemade soy sauce and chili oil on the table. Moo shu tofu was served an awesome hoisin sauce, but the tofu and vegetables themselves had a surprising, odd taste, almost like maple syrup, that nearly made me commit an uncharacteristic act of public spitting. Fresh, chocolate-filled doughnuts, on the house, ended the meal well. All in all, the inconsistent food, not-quite-smooth-yet service and highish prices make me wonder if this place will last any longer than its predecessor.

text: Alternative medicine, to my understanding, includes looking at someone with a holistic approach. Unfortunately my experience with Dr. Garcia was anything but holistic. Twenty minutes after my scheduled 10am appointment, Dr. Garcia escorted me back to his office. He sat at his office chair looking at the laptop on his lap and asked brusquely, "What are you here for?" This is the approach I would fully expect from a conventional doctor, but not from someone who practices alternative medicine. Since I am hypothyroid and need my prescription renewed, I need current blood work done. He suggested that this be done in his office right now. I'm not a medical expert, but I have had blood drawn several times a year for the past several years and EVERY time I'm told to not only fast, but also don't take my thyroid medication because it will throw off results. I was concerned and confused that Dr. Garcia was going to make a determination on my prescription with blood drawn right there on the spot. When I mentioned that my cortisol was very high a few years ago, Dr. Garcia made a sweeping statement that my adrenal system is shot. Again, an assumption I would expect from a conventional doctor. My expectation of someone who practices alternative medicine is that they would inquire about what external factors were going on in my life at that time, and what are your cortisol levels now? Had Dr. Garcia done that, he would have learned that I was going through a divorce at that time, and labs since then have shown that everything in that area is fine. At the end of our consultation he wrote a list on the back of a piece of scratch paper (I'm not making this up!), which included "diet and supplements" as my course of action, along with a number of treatments he offers. When I inquired about which supplements I should take, he said he sells a package. Again, I inquired about which supplements I should use, because I'm already taking a few things. Instead of giving me a clear answer he wanted me to list what I am taking and he'll let me know if I should take it or not. "Or you can just buy my package." I'm guessing he has considerable markup on his package and other office treatments. After about 45 minutes, I knew a lot about Dr. Garcia's view of mammography and thermography (how did that even come up?), about his supplements, about his other body cleanse services, about his cancer patients (the bulk of his business, it appears), and he knew very little about me or my life situation. How can a doctor take a holistic approach if they don't even have half of my story? I felt like I was just another dollar sign passing through his office, much like his terminal cancer patients. Unfortunately, I did make a considerable contribution to Utopia on this initial consultation, but I won't repeat that mistake. I thought I had done my research. Dr. Garcia's website said all of the right things. I wish I had had someone else's experience to draw on before making my appointment. Jim & Colette http://www.roamingtogether.com http://www.facebook.com/followrt

text: As a college student in New Orleans, I travel frequently in and out of this airport. The rates for Airport Shuttle are $15 one way, $30 round trip. Airport Shuttle tends to wait until the shuttles are COMPLETELY full, so you will have to wait 20 minutes to leave. It is not a very comfortable ride either-with everyone packed in with their luggage, things get a little cramped. In addition, Airport Shuttle takes everyone to different hotels, so you may have to go to several different hotels before you get to your final destination. A warning to Tulane and Loyola students-Airport Shuttle will drop off ALL the hotel people, THEN the university students. How excited were we?! Very. We grabbed a roof-top spot and readied ourselves for a dip back in time. We were ready. Still ready. Even more ready. Almost 20 minutes later, Joe Cool, our waiter strolled up to us and asked to get our drink order. Um hello!? That was merely the beginning. After ordering our bevs, we gave the go-ahead for the entree order as well. Obviously he couldn't handle it because he just walked away, even after I said loud and clear that we were "ready to order the rest!" So he comes back with our drinks, puts them down, and leaves again because he forgot straws. Eight minutes later, he returns, pen in hand! My parents, being the traditionalists they are, order two Hurricane specialties -- the grouper sandwich. "Oh we just ran out of grouper like 10 minutes ago," he informs us. Are you kidding?! Needless to say, they were out of almost everything we wanted (including the flounder), the meal was overpriced, over cooked, and not worth the drive. We left disappointed and brokenhearted to see what one of our favorite hot spots had turned into.
label: NEG

text: Hey there, Delilah, where's the pride? Quality? Value? Hiding in New York City? After garlic na'an, corn bread is my favorite type of bread in the entire world so I should have known to prepare myself for disappointment when my platter was served without corn bread and only the brief acknowledgment that it "wasn't ready yet." I ordered a quarter chicken platter with macaroni and cheese. The chicken was "ho hum" and lacked flavor, although it was fairly moist. The macaroni and cheese was tasty, but not exceptional. I didn't see how it was any different than the baked macaroni and cheese you can find in any urban cafeteria setting. Service was somewhat odd. After ordering, the two employees struggled to fill my party's orders while perplexedly staring at the receipt. My father's order was forgotten all together, but to the credit of the employees, he was given a free wing once his order was finally filled. I'm surprised that they didn't offer us a free side, drink or discount for the absence of the corn bread, which was never finished even after we took about 20 minutes to eat. I'm sure "Delilah" makes delicious food with lots of love, but it seems like her business has expanded too much and become just another place serving heaping portions of comfort foods from steam trays at high prices.
label: NEG

text: I originally planned on hitting up Old Nelson next door for some egg salad on a bagel... but lo and behold, NO BAGELS! When I want egg salad, it has to be on a bagel and it has to be NOW. :) So, while my coworkers waited at Old Nelson in a throng of hungry folks, I strolled next door to this little spot that I didn't even know existed. I am SO glad I found it because I cannot get over the delicious menu. I have yet to try something there that I don't like. There is plenty to choose from for a flexitarian (meaning, eats minimal meat) like me which is quite a departure from any other deli menu I've encountered. They serve breakfast food all day long and their latkes are to die for. That egg salad sandwich was just the beginning of my tour de Delicatessen! Since eating there just last week I have been back 3 (or is it 4 times) and have never been disappointed. Wholy Trinity (grilled muenster, avocado and tomato on rye) - YES!!! Nunziostein (pizza bagel with fresh mozz) - definitely!!! Chicken Matzo Ball -- pretty damn good Microbrew soda - Heck, why not!?!?! If you're in the area it's totally worth it! Staff is great and food is quick and delicious!

And the dimly lit individual-stall bathrooms are not pleasing. Palace still gets 5 stars, though, because you're not going to find a better Indian lunch in Center City; at least I haven't.

text: I'm from San Diego, so I have a lot of experience buying from and selling to consignment stores. I went there for the first time a few weeks ago. I was surprised by how small and cramped the store was. It looks like the back store room of a legitimate clothing store. The racks are packed with clothes organized in alternating methods (some racks by color, some by size, some by brand, etc.). With more than three people in the store--including associates--the store is overwhelming cramped. The clothes available for purchase are less than appealing to buy as second-hand (I personally wouldn't have bought half the clothes first-hand, either). The majority of the clothes are well-worn plain, solid colored tanks and tees. The quality and selection of the clothing and shoes is severely lacking. Additionally, the sizing is highly skewed to the size 10 (women's) and plus crowd. Any semblance of a brand name can be found on the packed three-foot hanger of jeans: size 10+ well-worn "7 for All Mankind" jeans. After being in the store for nearly fifteen minutes browsing, that is all I could find in the way of "high quality" and "brand name" clothing that The Closet so strongly advertises. The associates are relatively unpleasant and more interested in chatting with each other behind the register than assisting customers. They also seem extremely overstaffed for the tiny store space and minimal customer activity they experience. I would imagine that in the future, if The Closet survives, their selection in clothes will even out in size, brand, etc. However, for now, it appears as if they bought just about anything they could get their hands on to pack on their crowded racks. I would recommend heading down the road a few blocks to Nordstrom. Spend about $10 extra dollars and get a true brand name piece of clothing, not something that could have been sold first-hand for less at Forever 21.
label: NEG

text: So far, Woodlands is my favorite Indian restaurant in Nashville. I'm used to only having two or three vegetarian options to choose from when I eat out, so Woodlands was a welcome change. The service is good, and the two dishes and the naan we ordered were all so tasty that I wished they didnt' fill me up so quickly. Woodlands' prices are also lower than the average Indian restaurant, which is a plus, especially since you're still getting a high quality meal. I'd recommend trying to gulab jamman for desert - warm, doughy fried cheese balls soaked in sweet rose water, mmmmm. Other reviewers have criticized Woodlands' decor, but I think it has an appealingly quirky and interesting look, compared to the more proper Indian restaurants I've visited. The one drawback to Woodlands is that if your date is a steadfast omnivore, you'll have to go elsewhere.

text: I'm giving Wegmans their 5th star because of the insanely amazing produce they have sourced this summer. Seriously, they have more fresh, local food than I have ever seen at a Whole Foods. The tomatoes, peaches, corn, and neon eggplants have been a godsend for me, since I have been stuck in a cooking rut for the past couple months. The local tomatoes have been especially incredible- far and away the best I've ever had from a grocery store and better than I've had from some farmers markets lately. They are flavorful, meaty and have the perfect balance of sweetness and acid. Also, I recently made the mistake of sampling their ultimate white cake. Holy crap, I have never had a cake this good from a grocery store bakery. It wasn't overly sweet and the vanilla flavor was very strong- over all it is a rather adult treat.

text: I wanted to have a set of gel nails done and I went wandering around the city looking for a place that was open on a Sunday. I happened upon this place and their menu said they did UV gel nails. It was my first time at this salon and my first time getting UV gel nails. I asked them if they applied gel and let it heat cure with UV and they said yes that is how it worked. I sat down and May (I believe) started to work. She started to lay down acrylic on my nails and I had to stop her and ask what she was doing. She didn't understand my questions and had to ask the shop manager to come assist. It turns out that they don't do a true UV gel nail here. They lay down acrylic (supposedly special UV acrylic) and then a layer of gel on top to make it shiny. You do get the heat curing on the one layer of gel. I wasn't happy about this but figured I was already invested in it and decided to just go forward. I'd have acrylics in the past so they weren't foreign to me and I knew they were strong and decently long-lasting. The work was done fairly efficiently and looked decent from afar from when you look closer you see air bubbles, crooked nails, too much acrylic at the edges and in some spots fairly thick. OK, I can deal with all that shoddiness since it serves me right for trying to do this cheaper. BUT, it's now 3 days later and half the nails are lifting and I'm very unhappy about this. I will now have to go back to this salon to get them fixed or go somewhere else to have them removed and re-applied. I phoned them and was informed by a member of the staff that if they started having problems after 2 days they would charge me to fix them. But if it was before two days they'd try and correct it. I'm not particularly happy with this response. I will call again and speak to the manager.
label: NEG

text: My two girlfriends and I chose this little hidden gem for our monthly girls night outing, mainly because it's a BYOB. We arrived to the restaurant to find a huge, rowdy family birthday party finishing their dinner. We were promptly seated, our server was attentive and friendly, even though she was probably frazzled from the huge birthday party. The menu is split into 2 pages of Italian dishes and 1 page of Spanish dishes. We all went with Italian dishes, each ordering our own appetizers and entrees - I got the mussels in red sauce to start, they were delicious as mussels can be. For my main course, I got the black pasta with salmon and crabmeat. I am a sucker for homemade pasta and this was tasty and chock full of salmon and crabmeat. I sampled my friends' food - gnocchi, chicken marsala, and both were also good and homemade too. Our server deserved her hefty tip for being so attentive and always checking in with us even though she had a million other people to deal with, and seemed like the only server for the whole place. I would definitely come back and try their Spanish side of the menu! Best part is that it is so inexpensive (3 apps and 3 entrees for under $75) and BYOB.

text: You know what I love about my job? That I travel and am in a different city every week. And every other week I'm in a big city: NY, San Fran, Philly, Chicago, you get the idea. And I'm alone. So I eat what, where and when I want. No group of friends all with different appetites (although, I must admit the company would be nice) and no hubby ordering a bloody steak for every meal (and, being a veggie, that gets old and gross). So, I had a hunkering for Indian food tonight and decided to try Palace at the Ben. I braved 30ish degree weather to walk about 10 blocks to this place. I instantly noticed how sleek and chic this restaurant is: marbled columns (probably painted but beautiful), white linen table cloths and crystal chandeliers. The smell was amazing. I was seated immediately and had my drink within 3 minutes. The wait staff hops, and I mean runs, actually. I was in, ordered, ate and out in less then an hour. My meal was wonderful, I ordered the Panir Kulcha (naan filled with panir cheese and spices) and Navratan Korma (9 veggies slow simmered with cream sauce, raisins and nuts). Amazing! The veggie dish was cooked perfectly, the nuts gave a nice crunch and the sauce was creamy but had the perfect touch of spice. I washed it all down with a cool, sweet and frothy Mango Lassi. This place was amazing. I'm giving 4 out of 5 stars only because they don't offer a veggie sampler (which I am used to at the other Indian restaurants I have visited). I'd def recommend if you live around here or are just traveling for business. You won't be disappointed!!
label: POS

text: I recently went to a wedding that was catered by Russo's. The food was really, really good. The vegetable medley was prepared just right and cooked the perfect amount of time to make them not to mushy or to tough. I also loved the pork and for the more part, I don't eat a lot of pork (except bacon). It looked so good that I had to try it. The gravy was the perfect consistency and just a touch of it was excellent on the pork. The chicken was stuffed and a little dry, but everything else was so good that I barely noticed it. My date is a food snob and raved about the pork. He is no stranger to the finest restaurants in town, so I was a little nervous he would complain about the food. Not one complaint, except he agreed about the chicken being a little dry. I do not know if Russo's made the cake, but it was excellent. There was a chocolate cake with white icing. A white cake with white icing and creamy fudge in the middle. Also a white cake with white icing and strawberry filling. Being the dedicated Yelper that I am, I tried all of them!!! Just wanted to make sure I could give a full report :) I spoke to the bride and she said the process was super simple with Russo's. She had a tasting and decided what she wanted. She never had to think about any of it again until she had her meal the night of her wedding.

text: I heard about this place from a friend (@amandastewart) on Twitter. I am a huge fan of Salvador Dali. When I found out it was only 30 min away from where I was staying in Tampa, I had to go there. The drive from Tampa wasn't bad. The weather was perfect. Parking for the museum is available in two parking lots. The parking lot located next to the museum building is very small and packed. I had to park in the dirt/sand lot across the street. When you walk into the museum you are inside of the Dali store. Adult entry is $17. The store had plenty of Dali merchandise at reasonable prices. The museum features 6 of Dali's Masterworks. They are breathtaking. There are other works of art that Dali created, however I left wanting more. I thought there would be many more pieces on display. There are several guided tours available throughout the day. I tried to follow one, but it was too slow for me and I couldn't hear what the guide was saying. It was difficult to see the works of art during the tour, so that was another reason why I ditched the tour in favor of exploring on my own. Cameras and cell phones are not permitted inside the gallery area.

text: I was going to preface this review with a defense of Starbucks, but changed my mind and decided to not get into the politics and simply stick to reviewing. (Though I will say - politics does influence where I will spend my money.) In some ways, a Starbucks is a Starbucks. At least if you are at a Company Store and not a Licensed Location (of which there are thankfully few.) However, in the world of "the same" this location stands out as wonderful. The Baristas are uniquely friendly. They also do seem to try harder to be helpful than at other locations. I have on a few occasions needed to speak to a manager, not for problems, but to get information, and the woman who seems to be the store manager is knowledgeable and responsive. She also seems to have a good rapport with the staff, which may account for the quality of service. The store, and specifically the restroom, is always clean, and when I have found it lacking in a paper product, they are quick to fix the problem. Although the lines can be long, service doesn't dawdle. On the other hand, when it isn't busy, staff is happy to chat about coffee, or movies, if you are interested and don't interfere with their work getting done. There are plenty of tables, and four areas which have power outlets, which is more than most locations, so it is truly possible to be there and get work done. It does get crowded at times, especially during exam weeks at Drexel and Penn, but I have only once, out of many visits had to leave because I couldn't find a seat. text: Diagonally across grid-locked Route 70 from Han-Ah-Reum (or H-Mart), set back in the Barclay Shopping Center, is the Chinese answer to the Korean mega-mart. I think the Koreans have won. Not that there's nothing to like at the Asian Mart, mind you. For one, it's big. Which means plenty of varieties of instant noodles, canned pickled vegetables, fermented sauces and snacks. They have a five star snack section. Pocky! dried Mango! Salty Prunes! Dried Squid! For the same prices as you would see at Philly's C-town, the deli offers up decent roast pork, duck, soy sauce chicken, curried octopus and porcine offal. The small buy-by-the-pound hot foods section offers mapo doufu and braised pork butt. Just remember to get there early since most of the deli and hot foods are gone by mid-afternoon. Coincidentally, these are items that for obvious reasons, cannot be found at the Han-Ah_reum. Chinese 3, Koreans 0 But what could be a vibrant Asian market experience, turns flat when you visit the fresh veggies and fruit section, and their meat and fish markets. Sure you can get the usual Chinese veggies like Shanghai bai cai and Chinese broccoli and bitter melon, but they like to wrap everything in plastic bags (so that you can't pick certain things and they control the portion you buy). That really irks me. The H-Mart, on the other hand, has that laissez faire thing where I can choose which ever green bean I please and only get 3 ounces if I that's all I need. And, the veggies look fresh, unencumbered by the plastic bags. Chinese 3, Koreans 1. Both places have small fish sections where you can pick a living fish which they will give last rites to and clean it as well. I do find that the H-Mart have somewhat fresher iced fish than the Asian MArt. You can tell by the clarity in the fish's eyes. That is, if you can get yourself to look it in the eye. CHinese 3, Koreans 2. In the meat sections, they both have butchers on hand as well as prepackaged meats. But it's hard to find basic meats, like chicken legs and pork chops at the Asian Mart and often the meats behind the case don't look appetizing. The only time I bought any meat there was when spare ribs were on sale. If I need ground pork for dumplings (jiao zi) or mandoo, I brave crossing Rt. 70 to get to H-Mart. The Koreans have tied it up. But the main reason why I wind up saying "Annyong ha shimnikka" to the missionaries in the parking lot and head into H-Mart is the crispy, demurely sweet store-made rice treats. The stoic rice-cake man pops them out like nobody's business and the free samples keep my whiny kids sedate. Pop! There goes another rice cake. Pure theater! Koreans 4, Chinese 3. So, Asian market, you need loosen up a little. Free the vegetables from their clear plastic straight jackets! Get rid of the rigor mortised, bleary eyed fish on ice! Play on your strengths! Have a Pocky themed event! Cooking classes with durian! Show us that you can partay and we'll come.

text: I went to Tria this past weekend to meet up with some friends, a little early start to the night's Memorial Day weekend festivities. First, I mistakenly went to the 18th st. location, only to realize my friends were at the one on 12th & spruce...no matter, a quick cab ride got me there in no time. FIRST IMPRESSIONS: This place is clearly for the sophisticated crowd, as if there is a such thing as the unsophisticated wine and cheese bar (I won't ask). It's a place to go to enjoy a fine glass of wine and a small thing or two off the menu. It didn't strike me as a place to go for dinner, although this might not be the case...I had a couple glasses of the Four Graces Pinot Blanc, and the Italian Meats tray. THE LAYOUT: Sophisticated and refined are the key words here. It's not some lifestyles of the rich and famous kind of pomp-shack...but if you are put off by yuppies in sport coats laughing pretentiously at the toiling of the average lowly peon, this might not be the joint for you (okay, I didn't hear any laughing about said subject going on, but you get the point hopefully). Dark wooden furniture, lit naturally by the afternoon sun peering through the large open windows. There is a patio section and an indoor section, separated by these large windows, which are open in warmer months. THE WINE & FOOD: The reason I tried the Four Graces is because Tria does a special, pairing a selection of wine, cheeses, and beer, first round is half off. It was exquisite in my (unseasoned) opinion-- I was looking for a wine that wasn't too dry, a little fruity, and that held it's flavor and consistency throughout. Hit the nail on the head. The Italian Meat platter was also very good-- various Italian meats that I won't dare to try and remember the name/spelling, some of the sweetest red peppers I've ever seen, and a delicious mixture of garlic-infused olive oil with a tangy red pepper/garlic paste for the bread...oh yeah, and Caper Berries...I don't like them, so I won't allow it to affect my review, if you like em, you will probably enjoy them here. It was all very tasty, if not a little expensive (although not necessarily overpriced)...I wasn't expecting more for my money, per se, I was just surprised at the bill. It's not a killer, but it was a little high. THE SERVICE: We were fortunate enough to have Shuli (sp?) as our server, she was very friendly, attentive and knowledgeable. Sometimes when you visit a place like this, you get some hipster wine snob who expects you to know Napa like the back of your hand. Well in Shuli's case, despite my constant ignorant inadvertent insults to the finer things in life, she was able to boost my experience by being so nice. I don't know if it's a good thing or a bad thing that there isn't a set dress code for the staff there, but someone behind the bar was wearing a plaid shirt...not what I'd expect to see, but I don't get bothered by things like that. THE ATMOSPHERE: We spent the afternoon in a wine-induced haze (not drunk, mind you) feeling the buzz and the warm breeze. We talked about all kinds of things, including the VERY eclectic soundtrack, which went from kama sutra-esque ambient, to underground chill hip hop, to country, to pub rock. I don't know who the hell put together that playlist, but it drew more laughter than anything else-- the transitions were too abrupt. It didn't take away from the experience, but it was notable. THE VERDICT: If you are looking for a great, relaxing, refined experience, or if you want to throw (or enjoy) a wine and cheese party outside of your designer loft, Tria, is the place to go. I gave it 4 out of 5 for the minor annoyances I had (I'm like Larry David when it comes to wierd random quirks like that), but it really was an excellent way to start the evening, and I would love to go back again!
label: POS

text: Went for brunch today before taking advantage of Bank of America's first weekends at the Frist. I sampled the shrimp and grits. I have had this dish in a lot of places, and to me it's like making an omelet. If a place can make this anywhere close to my expectations, then I know I'll be back. Allium uses a lot of spice and pepper jack cheese to build a spicy, but not too hot flavor profile. If you start eating the dish right out of the kitchen, you will burn something in your mouth. Give it a second to cool and enjoy it properly. I could use more shrimp, but I could always use more shrimp. The grits stand up pretty well and, in spite of the on-the-small-side gulf shrimp used, it's an above average execution of a staple dish. I had some time before the museum opened, so I went ahead and indulged in desert. I had the creme brulee and, before I go any further, I must note that I often eat this dish with a brulee snob, so I have had it more times than any one man should. That notwithstanding, the dessert holds up to expectations. I did think that the texture was a little elementary and the sugar crust was a little thin (no satisfying "crack and crunch" when hit with the spoon) the flavor was there. After all, it's flavor we're after and Nashville isn't really known for its superior adherence to palatable textures. I look forward to going back and trying one of the Benedicts. I suggest you give it a try as well.

text: A few points to be made. Dyer Chiropractic has an attractive office, and is conveniently located... I went a handful of times... The first visit was nothing more than a consultation, which was a bit disappointing, as I had hoped to get an adjustment that day. As I said, I was dealing with some pretty bad headaches and I needed relief. He recommended that I go to a hospital to get some spinal x-rays, because I had not had any in a couple of years. I got them that evening, and hand delivered them to their office. One thing that made me a bit uncomfortable was the sense of forced Christianity while I was there. In a professional office, I expect for the interactions to be professional, and kinda surprised by the comments that he would make periodically. For example, at one point, he said to me, "Christ is great, isn't he?" Only, it wasn't a rhetorical question... He asked it again when I didn't respond the first time. This made for an awkward interaction because I feel that spirituality is a private matter and not something I need to be discussing with persons I barely know. Despite this, I made my first appointment, and things went fine enough. The next time I was there, I happened to be scheduled right after a woman who seemed to think that the chiropractor was also her therapist. She was in the next stall over, and talked and talked and talked. This went on for literally half an hour... all while I was sitting there waiting. He finally got to me and made no apologies for making me wait. I was willing to see this as a fluke, but it just so happened that my next appointment was ALSO scheduled just after this woman. This time, he was with her for even LONGER. I considered walking out, as my time is just as valuable as his, and anyone else's. Finally he made it to me, and he did apologise this time, telling me that, "Some people need a little more help." Fine. But we're all customers. I felt that he should have adjusted me first, and gotten me out of the way if he knew that this woman needed more "help" (i.e. time to chit chat.) Fast forward to three weeks ago. Despite tri-weekly visits to their office, no one had ever told me that I had an outstanding balance... but they finally got around to letting me know. My health fund had apparently run out, and the rest would be out-of-pocket. No big deal... But I would have like to be notified BEFORE two months of co-pays had accumulated. A week after that (two weeks ago) we received our first and ONLY bill from them. TODAY... I got a voicemail from their office asking me to take care of the "situation" with my bill, and telling me that they didn't want to have to turn me over to collections. I was floored. I had not had the bill in my hands for more than a couple weeks, and on top of that, I was still waiting to see if the insurance made any more payments before paying my balance. I feel insulted that they brought up turning me over to collections as though I was some sort of criminal. This is especially troubling considering the strong "Christian" message they seem to hold to so dearly. This is clearly another example an entity claiming to embrace Christian values while acting in a way that is contrary to that. As I said, I won't be back.

The end of the night came, and the next time we used the alcohol at home, the bottle was filled with water. The food was ok but nothing to write home about. It wasn't til I found an old video clip from Sesame Street, one of the most memorable of my childhood, that I realized why Mema's instantly found a special place in my heart. Check it: http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HkkSNP3ee0w. Highly recommended.

text: I have been a skeptical of the whole point on 'Dim Sum'. I don't like it because: 1. If I eat with friends, I ended up paying too much for a food that I didn't get to eat, because my friends ate em all. 2. I don't like the whole idea of me eating and being bothered every single second by the waiters/waitresses. 3. Their food is plain as it can be. However, last saturday I went with gf (in here for vacation), despite being skeptical about such place, since she was craving for it. The first 10 minutes after getting seated and start picking our foods, everything went very well. My point of view about dim sum about to be changed. I actually thought that it'd be nice if someday I take my parents to eat here and have a good family time together. But then.. after the 3rd and so on dish, I felt that the food was getting plain and plainer. And so, after we both full, we decided to pay for it. The cashier didn't smile. Didn't ask anything like hows the food etc etc. Didn't even say hi. Just take our check and cash. Gave us our change and didn't even say 'thank you'. As soon as the whole transaction was done and we're about to go, one of the waiter came to us in a hurry and this is what came out of his mouth 'you didn't leave tips'. At first I didn't quite catch that so I asked again, 'i'm sorry, what?'. He replied back 'you didn't leave tips..tips!' I was a bit baffled about it. But I was quick to response, so I took out $2 and gave it to him and hurried to leave the place at once. I was so shocked I can't even say anything. First of all, a restaurant did not supposed to ask for tips, not even to the point of chasing it's customer. Second of all, tipping are not required and it's something that is earned. Anyway not going to whine more. What's done is done. We won't be back at all. I won't ever bring my parents. My skepticism about dim sum will get stronger. Bottom line is this place is utterly sucks. If I can give no stars, I'd prefer that. $14.65 + $2 for 5 very small trays of food and tips extortion are not worth every penny.

text: The gaucho's way to prepare meat - even worth the week of restraint afterwards! ----- 1) As if you didn't already know, let's make one thing clear: Hire a babysitter for your vegetarian friends, or pretend you're meeting at Maoz instead. Ditto for "dainty" eaters - especially when you have to pick up the tab! 2) Now, in case you didn't know, I've been to this place as well as its half-baked competitor on JFK boulevard (which will remain nameless). I've never had a bad meal here at Fogo. Stream of consciousness - Those oddly-labeled bottles they blow through to make their caipirinhas? Yep, real-deal Brazilian cachaça. - I actually enjoy their cheese bread puffs, and their fried polenta. But if you fill up on this, and on the same token if you eat anything for 12 hours before your Fogo experience, you'll be sorry... - Who knew a simple 2-colored coaster (green light for "more beef!", red light for "Slow down, I'm about to commit a party foul!") had so much power? - They have multiple cuts of meat, ranging from the mundane (chicken drumsticks) to the sublime (leg of lamb, filet mignon). Some of the cuts include: Bacon-wrapped Filet mignon Regular filet mignon Sausage links Top round Bottom round Lamb leg Lamb chops Pork ribs etc... - You can usually specify done-ness (medium rare) and the servers usually do a good job of slicing the appropriate cut. Of course, it's an inexact science, considering they have no control of grill times for irregularly shaped meats - The meat is simply seasoned in salt, pepper, and perhaps a small bit of citrus. This is either too salty or too bland depending on your tastes. But this is all the more reason to get medium rare, to better appreciate the meat's quality. - The salad bar gets bonus points for not just being an afterthought. Shitake mushrooms, hearts of palm, smoked salmon, and a real Parmesan wheel are some of the highlights. I mean, when was the last time you had real Parmesan cheese? From a wheel? - Another plus is their rather extensive wine selection. Of course there are steakhouses with better wine selections, but you can't go wrong with a restaurant profiled in Wine Spectator. - Bring $$$$. Dinner is $50/person, not including alcohol, tax, tip. Our party of seven, with two mid-price reds (one cab, one malbec) came to almost 6 c-notes. Would I be back? HELLS YEA. Let me start fasting now.

text: You know that part in Kentucky Fried Movie where the operatives are talking about a shithole and one of them asks "Worse than Detroit?" Yeah, Tucson is that bad. Tucson is filled with dirt. That's the best way I can describe it. I observed it for EIGHTEEN YEARS. I should know. It is shades of brown. Slightly darker brown when the monsoons come, but dirt brown nonetheless. The sky is brownish blue, and depression is characterized as feeling "brown," not blue. The tap water is brown, bridal costumes are brown, you can buy any color car you wants as long as it's brown, and TV is broadcast in 256 shades of brown. The only thing NOT brown is the nasty-looking silver and turquoise patterned jewelry and decor that people call "southwestern." There are barrios everywhere covered in dirt and graffiti, smelling of defeat and resignation. It starts at the airport and reaches all the way to the foothills. Nothing grows in Tucson except cactus, gang violence, drug use and spousal abuse. Not even love can grow there. It's a stifling vacuum. Escape while you can. On the upside, there are lots of Mexicans. I mean Mexican restaurants. There's a cool museum or two and the UofA, and there's more desert than you can shake a sad, defeated stick at. Mt Lemmon can be pretty nice, and I have some fond memories of Summerhaven, picking berries in the mountains, and catching trout and crawdads in Rose Lake. Oh, and the sunsets are kind of nice, and the monsoons bring heavy warm rain and great lightning and thunderstorms. The best and worst thing is the airport: You're either coming or going. I hear it's a great place to retire. It's certainly a valid place in which one could expire. If you don't have an air conditioner, buy a gun. Oppressive only begins to cover it. The heat is literally deadly.

text: I took some time to read the other reviews before I wrote mine, so do not think the two stars is a snap judgment. Like many others, I've been coming to Zern's my entire life. I have been bringing my son there since he was born, and my 90+ year old Aunt tells stories of when it was new and in the middle of nowhere. But Zern's has changed, and not in a good way. I've watched the cafeteria close and never be replaced by a business that has stuck for more than a season. I've seen the flea market reduced from a huge venture to a few very old retailers hawking the same products they've been selling for the last ten years. Watched as craftsmen and real vendors have been replaced by dollar store vendors, siding salesmen, roof repair hawks, and empty stalls. Even the huge army navy store closed a couple years ago. replaced by a bunch of smaller craptastic hawkers. Spring Glenn farms, the last true purveyor of true PA Dutch food closed a few years back (Allentown Market Fair has a stall). There is only one Bakery left, and they are hit or miss with what they have, and Burts Farms, the best purveyor of meat in the market, closed this week. Years ago you'd see local farmers selling fresh produce along side their wives, who sold their jams, jellies, and fresh baked goods baked fresh early that morning. Do you remember? Zern's apparently does not. Yes - there are still some glimmers of hope. Little Richards, eternally staffed by teens still serves a decent lunch. The spice shop is well stocked and fair priced, and (some) of the fruit and veggie vendors still sell decent local produce. But the decent vendors are fast fleeing, and management seems content to let the market die. Maybe they'll put in a nice Wal*Mart - wouldn't that be grand?

text: Fei Yu-Ching was performing at the Peppermill, and my parents wanted to see him. My husband and I reserved two king size, no smoking beds through Hotels.com at Peppermill. We drove in at 5:30 PM to check-in. Front desk guy Jerome informed that they were upgrading one of our rooms to a suite, and downgrading one of our rooms to the travelodge that's connected with Peppermill. Hold up, "How about you don't downgrade us and just get us the rooms we reserved? It is import my parents and us stay together since my mom has Parkinsons." Jerome: "Nope, we don't have anymore rooms left." Me: "Then how come you accepted our booking?" Jerome: "That's hotels.com's fault. You didn't specify you wanted two rooms together." Me: "Can I speak with the manager?" Marian Ducett, the shift manager takes about 5 minutes to leisurely stroll over, doesn't make eye contact with me and says, "We don't have anymore rooms." Meanwhile, two more people next to me that came in after us checks-in gets a room in the Peppermill hotel. Me: "How come those people were able to check-in after us to get rooms?" M.D.: "Um... I believe they were checked into a high-roller's room they weren't suppose to be checked into. What do you want to do?" Me: "I just want my original booked rooms." M.D.: "Well I already told you we don't have those. You can go to another hotel if you want." I felt this establishment's employees slighted us. They clearly had rooms they were able to check us into, but were somehow informed to only upgrade one of our rooms and downgrade the other. We werent asking for neither rooms to be upgraded, we just wanted for the four of us to be in the same vincinity. Not at different towers and hotels. Furthermore, this upgraded "suite?" Ghetto Guady Hot Mess. Bomchigawahwah mirrors surrounding the entire room with disco lighting and a dingy hot tub right smack in the middle of it all on a platform. They might as well throw in a pole in that dang tub. We did get a refund for the downgraded room from Hotels.com and $25 food stamp from Peppermille (fine, they were food vouchers), but our trip was ruined. At the risk of my parents knowing we stayed at the a downgraded room and switching with us, we had to lie to them and say our room was across the hall and rush to meet them for breakfast the next day. Peppermill, odious.

text: Got the craving for some curry and saag paneer at lunch so I wandered on up to Samosa for some quick to-go grub. Walking into the small, plain restaurant, you can clock it for what it is; cheap bland Indian. My brain told me to leave but unfortunately my hunger compelled me to stay. Yes it's cheap but I can't really call it a bargain as you're getting what you pay for, certainly not bang for your buck. Here, little money gets you: little flavor, limited buffet selections, and samosas with an ever-hardening outer layer generated by hours under the heat lamp. Good Indian food possesses a powerful profile of flavors, and sometimes some nice heat; none of that here. Staff, when rarely around, not really helpful or pleasant; one guy in line at the buffet asked for a new set of tongs as he had fumbled them and caught them with his hand (on the part that grabs the food). The waiter decided not to fetch a fresh pair and that was my cue to leave. Unfortunately, not too many great Indian spots in the area and Samosa brings up the bottom of the list. Hell; they're name is Samosa and their samosas were damn weak. I've had better from the freezer.

text: Time - an awesome destination. When you walk in there are two options - to the left to enjoy some live jazz, or to the right to enjoy more of a swanky restaurant/bar that had some flat panels and some sort of music in the background. Both sections had nice crowds for a Wednesday night, but my friends and I (we were 5 total) opted right and grabbed open seats at the bar. Great vibe, cool decor - we were immediately greeted by one of the most extroverted bartenders I've ever been served by. The dude was super friendly and was great with offering drink and food recommendations. At some point he was fully involved in the conversation we were having and it was as though he were out with us; some may not like this, but this guy was cool enough where you'd be fine with it. Great beer selection - had some stuff on tap you won't find at many other places. Big whiskey selection too, though I hate whiskey. Had what seemed to be all of your standard bar fare, but all the menu items offered their own Time flare. Between the five of us, we ordered the stuffed clams, burger, vegetables, mussels, and wings. I had the vegetables, and boy, do you get your share of vegetables. Served tempura style, they provide a generous serving of cauliflower, carrots, zucchini, mushrooms, and some other tasty treats that I can't recall / identify. Ketchup, mayo-ish, and some Indian-esque sauce were served on the side. Very tasty, but it ended up being too much fried food for me. Everyone else loved their meals, and the mussels comes with a FULL PLATE of fries, and I do mean its own dedicated plate of fries piled high. Two beers and the veggies ran me 35 bucks - maybe a bit pricey but the experience was worth it. The live jazz section was really happening by the time we left, and I really wanted to check it out, but the night was over for me. I'll definitely go back, and this is a must for anyone who enjoys good live music (jazz is good music, I don't care what you think).
label: POS

text: When you enter the 4th Avenue location with floor to ceiling windows the ambient light and large colored tile concrete floors immediately give way to thoughts of an Art Gallery. WIth Canvas Oil Paintings, Illustrated Prints, Professional Sketches, and a T-Rex sculpture in view you immediately might forget this is a tattoo parlor. The staff is not your typical coffee monkey scenester kid, these pros are illustrators and accomplished artists who happen to be tattoo artists. Felix the mastermind at the establishment walks you through all stages of your tattoo with the patience of Buddha and the wisdom of Socrates. His casual nature lends the air that he knows more about tattoos than is responsible for one individual to know, and he does. The shop is very professional, clean, and in the heart of 4th avenue. You wont find rando college kids here looking for a drunk Chi Oh tattoo(in fact I hope they turn you away) or some other flash bullshit. This place is about integrity and honest work. Come with your thoughts and they will draw them out for a small fee. This is a shop owned and operated by artists, not ink junkies and random "i like to draw people" who picked up an electronic needle. Come for the art stay for a tattoo. Piercing's also available.
